text.approach: Reached from the Tank Lakes side of the Alpine Lakes high route, via the Foss River trails, not from Chetwoot Lake.
text.descent: Reverse the ascent: down the north ridge, round the northeast nose, and across talus to the saddle below the Tank Lakes plateau.

text.approach: Access is from the south, through the Jerry Lakes basin. From the Canyon Creek Trailhead (~1,900 ft, SR 20 near MP 141), ford Canyon Creek and take the McMillan Park-Jackita Ridge Trail #738 to the Crater Mountain trail, continue past Crater Lake, then leave the trail between about 6,400 and 6,700 ft for a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, cross the Jerry Glacier and drop into the Jerry Lakes basin, where nearly everyone camps; the route starts low on the glacier on the east side of the mountain, several hundred feet down into the next basin north. Most parties on Jack take three to four days for any route. No turn-by-turn approach exists for the East Ridge itself, so study satellite imagery before committing to a line. In July, from the Jerry Lakes camp a goat path leads to the col; lose about 800 ft into the next basin, climb the southeast arm, cross a snowfield and scramble to the ridge near 7,200 ft.

text.overview: A long, exposed rock ridge on the east side of Jack Mountain, mostly class 3 and 4 on loose greenstone with up to three short roped steps of low fifth class (the hardest about 5.0). Parties carry a rope and a few pieces for those steps and for protecting the downclimb.
text.descent: The East Ridge is one of the mountain's more reasonable descents — at least one documented party climbed the North Ridge specifically so they could descend this ridge. Reversing it means downclimbing sustained Class 4 on loose rock with big exposure, so carry enough slings and cord to leave rappel anchors on blocks where downclimbing is unattractive. text.approach: From Marblemount on WA-20, drive the Cascade River Road (FR-15) about 19-21 miles (paved to roughly mile 10, then gravel/washboard) to the Eldorado trailhead (~2,150 ft). Cross the North Fork Cascade River and follow the unmaintained Eldorado climbers' trail through forest and a boulder field to treeline, then to Eldorado Basin/Roush Creek camps (~6,000-6,300 ft). Ascend the Eldorado Glacier snow dome to the ~7,500-ft notch on Eldorado's lower East Ridge, traverse ~1.5 miles north across the upper Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col (7,800 ft), then continue easily to the nearby Klawatti-Austera Col (7,900 ft) to start the ridge.

text.overview: A Class 3 scramble along Klawatti's north ridge from the Klawatti-Austera Col, working around a rock tower nicknamed 'The Smokestack' before finishing on the summit crest.
text.descent: Downclimb the ridge crest back around The Smokestack via its west-side gully, return to the Klawatti-Austera Col, then to Klawatti Col. From there re-cross the Inspiration Glacier to the notch on Eldorado's East Ridge, descend the Eldorado Glacier, and follow the climbers' trail to the trailhead.

text.approach: Same trailhead as the Classic Route: park at the Reflection Lake pullout on Stevens Canyon Road when it's open, or at the Narada Falls pullout in winter/spring when the road is snow-gated (a short, steep ~200 ft climb from Narada Falls regains the road). Walk the road about half a mile to the 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest toward Tatoosh Creek (~4,500 ft), as with the Classic Route. Rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, stay low and work into the basin directly below Lane Peak's north face — the Zipper is the obvious left-leaning couloir splitting the center of the face, visible from the road. From the basin, hike up and across a large triangular apron of avalanche/rockfall debris fanning down from the base of the couloir. From the top of this debris cone, angle climber's left and climb roughly 1,000 ft up the couloir itself to a dead tree at a notch in the peak's east ridge, which marks the top of the technical climbing and the rappel/tie-in point. Snow conditions range from styrofoam neve to alpine ice depending on season and aspect; the basin and lower couloir cross avalanche-prone terrain, so this is a start-early, check-the-forecast approach, especially in winter/spring when most ascents happen. Total approach is roughly 2-2.5 miles one-way from the road to the notch; no water past Tatoosh Creek. In the couloir itself, expect the angle to build from about 40° to 45° near the top, the walls narrowing from roughly 40 ft to 20 ft wide

text.overview: Lane Peak's north face holds three couloirs; The Zipper, the central and most popular line, is the classic short winter/spring ice-and-snow climb in the Tatoosh Range. It climbs directly up a narrowing gully (about 40 ft wide lower down, pinching to ~20 ft near the top) that steepens from ~40° to ~45°, with a few short ice or mixed steps depending on conditions.
text.descent: Two descent options are used depending on conditions and whether the party continues to the true summit. Direct reversal (the usual bail line): from the dead-tree notch atop the couloir, downclimb a short stretch of exposed terrain to the tree, which carries fixed rappel slings (a natural, sling-on-tree anchor — not bolted), and make one rappel back down into the Zipper. waypoints.directions: From the Nisqually Entrance of Mount Rainier National Park, drive about 15 miles past Longmire toward Paradise and bear right onto Stevens Canyon Road. The Reflection Lakes parking is about 1.5 miles on, with the trailhead across the road. A park entrance pass is required. Stevens Canyon Road is closed roughly November to May; then park at Narada Falls and climb about 200 ft through the timber to regain the road.

waypoints.name: Lane Peak - Zipper couloir
waypoints.note: The Zipper is the left-leaning ~45-degree couloir at the center of the north face; ice axe/crampons required.
waypoints.directions: Walk Stevens Canyon Road west about half a mile to its 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. Stay low into the basin under Lane Peak's north face rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, cross the debris apron, and from its top angle left into the Zipper, the middle of three couloirs: about 1,000 ft of 40 to 45 degree snow with short steps to a dead tree at a notch in the east ridge.

text.approach: Same as The Zipper: From Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road (1.5 miles before Snow Lakes Trailhead), hike about 2 miles. Walk briefly along Stevens Canyon Road, then drop into basin toward Tatoosh Creek. Climb up debris triangle and continue to base of couloir system. Identify The Fly as the rightmost/broadest of the three couloirs. Approach takes approximately 45-75 minutes to couloir base.

text.overview: The Fly is the easiest and broadest of Lane Peak's three north-face couloirs. Instead of the Zipper's narrow center line, it climbs a wide gully trending right to a notch in the west ridge, from which most parties continue onto the standard South Face route rather than descending the way they came.
text.descent: From the top of the Fly at the west-ridge notch, most parties continue around onto the South Face and descend the standard 3rd/4th-class gully route rather than reversing the couloir. Rappelling or downclimbing the Fly itself is also done, particularly by skiers.

waypoints.name: Lane Peak - The Fly couloir
waypoints.note: The Fly is the broad, easiest couloir at the base of the face, trending right to a notch in the west ridge.
waypoints.directions: Walk the road a short way, then drop south into the basin toward Tatoosh Creek and climb the debris triangle to the base of the north-face couloirs, about 45 to 75 minutes. The Fly is the rightmost and broadest of the three, 40 to 50 ft wide; climb it at about 45 degrees, trending slightly right, as it eases to 30 to 35 degrees near its top at the notch in the west ridge.

text.approach: Identical to the Lemah Glacier approach, which is the only documented way into this cirque. From I-90 exit 80 (Roslyn / Salmon la Sac) go north on Bullfrog Road 2.8 miles through two roundabouts, continue on WA-903 past Cle Elum Lake (about 16.8 miles total from the freeway), turn west on FR-46 and follow it roughly 4.7-5 miles, then turn right on FR-4616 for 1-1.5 miles to the Pete Lake trailhead at about 2,800 ft (47.4350, -121.1855). Hike Cooper River / Pete Lake Trail 1323 about 4.4 flat miles to Pete Lake (2,979 ft), continue about 1.3 miles to a junction and stay right without crossing the creek, then 0.8 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn left (south) on the PCT for about 0.8 miles to Lemah Creek at roughly 3,200 ft; the PCT bridge over South Lemah Creek washed out in the winter of 2007/08 and parties still cross on a log about 20 yards downstream. Leave the trail at the creekside campsite and follow an old flagged climbers' path on the north side of Lemah Creek, with moderate alder and vine-maple bushwhacking, gaining about 400 ft in half a mile to the lower grassy meadow near 3,600 ft. Continue up dry stream beds toward the large snow finger and into the cirque below Lemah Two's east side; the towers on the east spur are directly above.

text.approach: Same start as the East Face: from SR-20, park at the informal pullout on the north shoulder of the highway a short walk east of the small pond, about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass (no permit needed). A well-beaten climbers' trail leaves the east end of the pond and climbs steeply through timber; in roughly 30 minutes it breaks out at the edge of the large boulder/talus field that lines the eastern base of the Liberty Bell group (Liberty Bell, Minuteman, Concord and Lexington Towers). From there, work up and left across the talus toward Lexington Tower's east side — 30-45 minutes total from the car to the base for most parties. There is no reliable water source along this approach (the roadside pond is not a water source worth using); carry what you need from the car. Snow can linger in the talus and at the base of the wall into early-mid summer and affects whether you gain the treed ledge from the left or right side. To reach the ledge itself, either climb a roped 5.8 pitch around a protruding block, or scramble one of the gullies flanking the ledge — both gullies see fairly frequent rockfall, so helmet up well before committing to them. Tooth and Claw begins near the left side of the treed ledge and angles rightward across slabs to the first bolt.

text.overview: Tooth and Claw climbs the steep, sustained slabs directly right of the East Face, giving Lexington Tower's hardest free line at 5.12a. It is more pure slab/edge climbing and considerably less traveled than the neighboring wide-crack testpieces, first climbed by Steve Risse and Dave Tower in 1989.
text.descent: Two real options, and most parties take the walk-off. Option 1 (walk-off): from the East Shoulder, make an exposed, somewhat sketchy 4th-class traverse west (it borders on unprotected 5th-class slab in spots, so many parties stay roped) to gain the same descent gully used off the East Face. waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin / Pond Pullout (east of Washington Pass)
waypoints.directions: Park at the informal pullout on the north shoulder of SR-20, about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass and a short walk east of the small roadside pond — the same start used for the East Face. No permit is needed here.

waypoints.name: Treed ledge (start of the route)
waypoints.note: Start on cracks and flakes from the left side of the treed ledge; the route moves right across slab toward the first bolt, often marked by a scrap of webbing, while the East Face exits left.
waypoints.directions: From the pond, follow the well-beaten climbers' trail steeply up through timber for about 30 minutes to the talus field under the Liberty Bell group, then work up and left across the talus to Lexington Tower's east side. Gain the treed ledge either by a roped pitch of about 5.8 around a protruding block or by one of the gullies on its north or south side; both gullies see frequent rockfall, and the snow and moat at the base decide which works.

waypoints.name: Lexington Tower East Shoulder (topout)
waypoints.note: This route climbs the slabs right of the East Face route on Lexington Tower, Washington Pass.
waypoints.directions: Climb seven pitches of slab and crack, with the 5.12a crux on the fifth, to the final bolted anchor, then scramble onto the East Shoulder. The climb ends here rather than on the main summit; walk off with the exposed fourth-class traverse west to the East Face descent gully, or rappel the route.

text.approach: Same East Face approach as the other Liberty Crack-area routes: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus. Liberty and Injustice for All takes a line roughly 10 meters right of Thin Red Line, so locate the correct start among the cluster of East Face lines (it shares some climbing with the old aid route Liberty Loop).

text.overview: Climbs the East Face about 10m right of Thin Red Line, joining it at Thin Red Line's seventh-pitch anchor. Established in 2014 by Mikey Schaefer, who rope-soloed the line. Technical, well-protected climbing on solid edges and thin crack features, with short bouldery 5.12- cruxes near the start of a couple of pitches leading to progressively easier climbing above — one of the more popular hard free lines on the wall.
text.descent: Rappel the route with two ropes; the descent is straightforward and every station is a two-bolt anchor with fixed biners. From the top of pitch 5, where the route joins the top of pitch 7 on Thin Red Line, rappel to the pitch-4 anchor and then to pitch 3. waypoints.note: Pullout at the SR-20 hairpin east of Washington Pass; walk back toward the pass to the pond where the East Face climbers' path starts.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Washington Pass and continue east down from the pass to the big hairpin turn below Liberty Bell's East Face, at about 5,200 ft; coming from Winthrop it is the hairpin just before the final climb to the pass. Park on the shoulder at the curve, then walk back up the road toward the pass to a small pond on the south side, where the climbers' path starts at its east end. SR-20 is closed over the pass in winter.

waypoints.note: The route ends here, about 650 ft up the East Face, where it joins Thin Red Line. Continue on Thin Red Line or rappel this route with two ropes; it does not reach the summit.
waypoints.directions: Walk back up SR-20 to the pond, round its east end and follow the cairned climbers' path about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face. Find Thin Red Line and start about 10 m to its right, then climb five pitches on two-bolt anchors to the Thin Red Line pitch-7 anchor.

text.approach: The X Couloir is most directly approached from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38); the less direct alternative starts at Heliotrope Ridge and reaches the southwest face through the Thunder Glacier cirque. Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start hiking/bushwhacking the old decommissioned road around Pt. 4481 toward Rankin Creek — snow travel (often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch) leads past East Rankin Lake (~5,120 ft) and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, near the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. From camp, an alpine start gets the team into the southwest basin and across the bergschrund crux while it's still cold and firm, climbing roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40° snow and a steep serac step in the X Couloir to the 9,085 ft summit. Total approach is on the order of 7 miles and 3,350 ft of gain to the basin camp. text.overview: Lincoln Peak's SW Face route, known as the 'X Couloir' (sometimes referenced as 'X Couloir – Emancipation Proclamation'), is the historic line up this seldom-climbed, seriously loose Black Buttes summit. First climbed by Fred Beckey, Wesley Grande, John Rupley, and Herb Staley on July 22, 1956, it was the only documented route to the summit until a 2015 first ascent opened a second line on the NW Face. Only about a dozen ascents are known; the peak is guarded by near-vertical walls on every side
text.descent: Most parties reverse the ascent line, downclimbing and rappelling the same southwest gully/couloir system (the X Couloir) back down into the southwest basin below the face. text.approach: From Highway 97 south of the Y-junction, drive ~7.5 miles and turn onto Ingalls Creek Road/Trailhead. Hike the Ingalls Creek Trail roughly 8 miles, then leave the trail (right/north) into brushy terrain up Crystal Creek, gaining about 2,200 ft to a base-camp meadow and tarn near 6,000 ft. From the tarn, climb a large talus-apron gully west of the tarn to a col at roughly 7,700-7,880 ft between Little Annapurna and the spires to its south.

text.overview: A rarely-climbed, two-pitch 5.5-5.6 rock route straight up Little Annapurna's steep true south face, approached from the seldom-used Ingalls Creek/Crystal Creek side rather than the Enchantments basin.
text.descent: From the summit plateau, descend north/northeast down talus and slab slopes toward Crystal Lake, then pick up the outlet stream drainage and follow it back down to the Crystal Creek base-camp meadow/tarn, retracing the approach back to Ingalls Creek Trail.

text.approach: Elbow Lake Trailhead, cross the Middle Fork Nooksack (unofficial log crossing recommended), off-trail through brush to Green Creek, cross Green Creek, ascend the rock buttress near 3,800 ft, then travel the Green Creek Glacier — staying on the lookers-left (south) side — up to the Cinderella-Little Sister col to start the ridge.

text.overview: A classic, moderate ridge line beginning at the Cinderella-Little Sister col: exposed low-5th-class climbing on excellent rock along a wild, jagged crest, finishing through looser 4th-class terrain to the summit.
text.descent: Most parties downclimb the same ridge back to the Cinderella-Little Sister col. An alternative is to drop onto the North Face side and rappel scattered fixed pin/tat anchors back to the Green Creek Glacier.

text.approach: From US Highway 2 at milepost 42 in the town of Baring (directly across from Der Baring Store), turn north onto Barclay Creek Road, Forest Service Road 6024, cross the BNSF railroad tracks and bear left at the fork about 0.2 miles up. Follow FS 6024 roughly 4.3–4.5 miles of gravel to the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft, where there is parking for roughly 20 cars, a vault toilet and picnic tables but no potable water. Walk Barclay Creek Trail 1055 east up the valley — it is a gentle, well-graded 2.2 miles to Barclay Lake at about 2,420 ft, directly under the wall. The footlog over Barclay Creek about 1.2 miles in has been removed, so expect to ford the creek until it is replaced; check current trail status. The north face rises straight out of the lake basin: 3,703 vertical feet from the lake to the summit in only half a mile of horizontal distance. Leave the trail near the lake and fight up the steep forested and brushy hillside beneath the wall — the first ascent of this face in 1960 found the first 1,000 feet to be exactly that kind of brush-and-forest struggle to reach a camp below the couloirs, and nothing about that terrain has improved since. There is no maintained climbers' path to the base of the main-peak wall (the fixed lines and boot track that exist on this mountain belong to the Dolomite Tower approach, which breaks off the trail well before the lake and heads up a different drainage). text.overview: A 14-pitch, Grade V 5.11c line up a roughly 2,600-ft section of Baring's north face, established in September 1992.
text.descent: There is no rappel descent of the north face. From the summit, follow the base-jumper boot track down and west for a few minutes, then swing counterclockwise toward the talus and drop into the notch between the north and south summits at roughly 5,550–5,600 ft. waypoints.name: Barclay Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From US 2 in Baring, directly across from the store, turn north onto 635th Place NE, cross the railroad tracks and keep left at the junction about 0.3 mile up, where the road becomes FS Road 6024. Follow the potholed gravel about 4 more miles to the Barclay Lake trailhead, with parking for about 20 cars and a vault toilet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.
